title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers are using generative AI to create deepfakes and impersonate real people to defraud victims. The deployment failure is that voice cloning, video synthesis, and phone spoofing technology can be obtained and applied to fraud with minimal barriers. Catching this would have required the AI systems used for voice synthesis and video generation to include detection mechanisms, watermarking, or hard limits preventing their use for impersonation.

The specific harm shows how AI-enabled impersonation amplifies traditional fraud schemes. A South Florida immigration attorney had his voice cloned to target immigrants seeking legal services. Victims reported losses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Voice cloning and deepfake creation tools exist in forms accessible to criminals, and detection at the point of use—by banks, phone systems, or platforms—was not established to stop the fraud.

It is not established how the criminals obtained the AI tools, whether any platform or service failed to detect or block the fraud, or what specific generative AI systems were used.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and impersonate trusted individuals in order to steal money from victims. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice was cloned to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints totaling over $10.4 million.

Scammers are using generative AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research family relationships to make fraudulent requests seem authentic. The technology has made traditional scams such as romance schemes, investment fraud, and grandparent scams far more believable. To protect themselves, consumers should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests by calling directly using known numbers, and avoid sending money based solely on phone calls or voicemails. Banks recommend pausing before responding to unexpected requests and monitoring accounts closely.
